The thesis

Life support is infrastructure. We are building it.

Every closed habitat, from a contaminated field site on Earth to a base on the Moon, lives or dies on one question: does the system stay in balance when no one is watching? For thirty years that question was answered by hand, slowly and expensively. We answer it with a single inference engine that closes the budget in real time, and we prove it at every scale before we trust it with a crew.

The engine

One Bayesian inference engine. On the edge.

Living systems are noisy, partly observed, and never quite at steady state. Our engine treats every reading as evidence, holding a probability distribution over the system's true state and continuously closing its mass and energy budget. It does not just log what happened. It estimates what is happening now and what is likely next, with calibrated uncertainty.

We compile that engine to run on edge-compute AI inside each product. Sensing, inference, and action happen on the device, with no cloud in the loop, so any system can decide and act autonomously, even offline. The same framework scales from a desktop vessel to a lunar habitat.

The stages

Proven at every scale before it carries a life.

From a sealed box on a bench to a room, to a flagship life-support core, to the field, to the Moon. Each stage validates the one above it.

STAGE 01
Benchtop · Synthetic

Digital Benchtop Gaia

It starts on a bench. A sensor-dense micro-biome runs alongside its digital twin, every flux instrumented and mirrored in simulation. You can run, perturb, and forecast a closed system at lab scale. This is where a hypothesis is tested before it ever touches a larger build.

STAGE 02
Aquaculture · Subsystems

Aquaculture Systems

Add a food and water loop. Recirculating aquaculture and aquaponic stacks run fish, biofilter, and grow bed as one managed nitrogen cycle, with modular dosing, filtration, and monitoring nodes that plug into any Gaia. The engine holds water chemistry in band and flags drift before it becomes a loss.

Gaia BLSS

STAGE 05
Terrestrial · Field

Mycroft

Take it outside. Mycroft is an autonomous rover that remediates contaminated ground with living systems. It senses, doses, and verifies the cleanup of soil and water in the field, on its own. This is the mud end of the arc: the same budget-closing engine, earning its keep on Earth today.

The endgame

Gaia BLSS, operational on the Moon.

The moon end of the arc. A crew-rated, edge-controlled closed loop keeping people alive off-world, running the exact framework we hardened on a bench and in the field. Earth is the proving ground. The Moon is the point.

Why we are doing this

Closing the loop is the whole game, here and there.

A system that can keep a crew alive on the Moon is the same system that can restore a poisoned watershed, feed a community from a sealed footprint, or hold a research biome stable for years. Closed living systems are the shared infrastructure of a livable Earth and an expanded human future. We are not picking between the mud and the moon. We are building the one thing both need, and proving it works before it has to.

The ask

What we are raising, and what it builds.

We are raising a seed round of $1.5M with a 15-month runway, to take the Bayesian engine from validated benchtop and research systems to a deployable Gaia BLSS core, and to put Mycroft into paid field pilots. The capital funds the jump from proof to product.
